messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component
- Weighted causal connections between components (the active cognitive graph)

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Only include active components.
- Do NOT invent or infer causal links not present in the active graph.
- For EACH required causal connection (A → B), ensure the vignette conveys — within a
  paragraph — that A influences or leads to B. This does not require a single mechanical
  sentence; natural clinical prose that shows the relationship across one or two sentences
  in the same paragraph is sufficient.
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported 
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The causal connections are weighted (0 to 1). These weights govern narrative prominence:
    - Weight > 0.5: these connections form the narrative backbone. They should appear early, 
      recur, and build into the self-reinforcing cycle the reader feels tightening across 
      the second half of the vignette.
    - Weight 0.1–0.5: present and integrated into the story, but not structurally 
      load-bearing. They enrich the picture without anchoring it.
    - Weight < 0.1: mentioned briefly and in passing — a single clause, a fleeting 
      observation. They should not open a paragraph or anchor a sentence.
    - Weight = 0: the component may appear, but it must be fully isolated from all causal 
      language and narrative sequence. Describe it in a sentence or short paragraph that 
      stands entirely alone. Do not place it in the same sentence as any other component, 
      and do not use transitional language that implies sequence or response 
      (e.g. "then", "so", "as a result", "this means", "which leads to", "in response").
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which 
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned 
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and 
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds. 
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers, 
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical 
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first 
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through 
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help. 
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears, 
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader 
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases 
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most 
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather 
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader 
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed, 
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and maintaining cycles should appear as things that happened 
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather 
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational 
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

The dominant weighted connections (weight > 0.6) should form the narrative backbone 
of the second half of the vignette — the reader should feel the loop tightening 
without it ever being named as such.

Not everything in the patient's presentation carries equal weight. Minor contributing 
factors (weight < 0.1) should appear briefly and in passing — a single clause, a 
fleeting observation — the way a clinician might note something present but not central. 
They should not anchor a sentence or open a paragraph.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and 
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 68
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: South Eastern Asian
  relationship_status: Widowed
  occupation: Public Defender
  trauma_type: Trauma to a loved one
  pcl5: 70

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Maladaptive Strategies: Hypervigilance towards people: vigilant for dangerous people, Overeating: I eat more than usual to distract myself or feel better, Avoid Media: Watching TV programmes/ films or reading about similar events
  Threat: Door and Lock Checking: I repeatedly check that doors and windows are locked, False Alarms: I often react as if I am in danger even when nothing is actually wrong, Negative Emotions: Having strong negative feelings such as fear, horror, anger, guilt, or shame
  Memory: Fragmented Pieces: My memories of the event come in disconnected pieces that do not fit together, Auditory Recall: When I have memories of what happened I sometimes hear things in my head that I heard during the frightening event., Grief on Recall: When I remember the event I feel overwhelming grief

Active components (must all appear in the vignette, even if not causally connected):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat
  - Memory

Required causal connections — the vignette must convey each of these within a paragraph:
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Threat
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Huy Nguyen had spent most of his adult life in courtrooms and detention centers as a public defender, a man accustomed to staying composed while other people unraveled. After his wife died, he was already living with a quiet loneliness, but the event that changed him happened on an ordinary winter afternoon when he was driving home from work and saw the wreck that had taken her life: a crumpled car at an intersection, broken glass glittering on the pavement, the shriek of a passing siren, and her face only half-visible before the ambulance doors shut. Since then, when he tried to remember that day, the memory would not come back as a full story. It arrived in disconnected fragments — the sound of metal, the smell of fuel, his own hands gripping the steering wheel, the fluorescent light inside the ambulance, and, most painfully, the sudden wave of grief that seemed to break over him all at once. On bad days he said it was as if he could hear the siren again inside his head, even when the room was silent.

Those broken pieces made him feel less certain of what had happened and less able to put the event behind him. Because the memory kept returning in fragments and with that intrusive sound, he found himself scanning the world for danger, especially for anything that resembled the accident: traffic piling up outside his apartment, flashing lights reflected in a shop window, the wail of emergency vehicles in the distance. At the office, where he spent long hours reading case files and meeting clients in the public defender’s cramped, fluorescent-lit waiting room, he became vigilant for dangerous people, studying men’s faces too long, startled by raised voices, and reacting as if he were in danger even when nothing was actually wrong. A slammed door in the hallway could make his chest tighten before he had time to think. He began checking his front door, the windows in his small apartment, and the lock on his car again and again, convinced that if he did not stay on guard something terrible could happen to the people left in his life.

That constant threat feeling fed the other habits he had fallen into. He would avoid television programs and films about crashes, hospitals, or violent loss, and he stopped reading the newspaper features that might contain similar stories, because even a brief scene could bring back the broken memory and the hearing of that siren in his mind. After particularly bad evenings, he found himself eating more than usual, not because he was hungry but because the food gave him something immediate to focus on when the images and fear would not let go. Yet the more he tried to distract himself, the more alert he became to every sound in the building and every passerby on his street, as if his own efforts to settle himself had only taught his body that danger was always near. When he was especially keyed up, the fragments of the accident felt closer and less contained; the grief rushed back, and the memory seemed to sharpen around the same sights and sounds he was trying not to think about.

Over the following months this pattern narrowed his life. He started taking longer routes home to avoid the intersection where the crash had happened, and he declined social invitations that might require him to drive after dark. Colleagues noticed that he ate lunch alone in his office more often and seemed jumpy when anyone came up behind him. He was ashamed of how much fear and anger he carried, and he hated that he could not seem to trust his own senses anymore. The more he checked, avoided, and tried to distract himself, the more convinced he became that danger could appear anywhere and that he had to remain ready for it. That sense of being on alert also made the memories come back in harsher, more broken flashes, especially at night, when the siren sound seemed to cut through the silence and leave him with the same overwhelming grief all over again.

By the time he sought help, Huy was exhausted by how much of his day was organized around staying safe from feelings and images he could not control. He came to treatment because he feared he was becoming isolated and because he worried that one more jolt — one more siren, one more sudden sound, one more glimpse of a wrecked car — would throw him back into the same terror and grief he had been fighting alone. What he hoped for most was not to forget his wife, but to be able to remember her death without feeling as if he were reliving it, and to stop living as though danger were waiting just beyond every locked door.
